date_and_recency: Study 1: published May 2019; 40-minute simulated drive; collection dates not stated in what was read. Study 2: received Sept 2022, accepted March 2023, online May 2023; 45-minute video-based simulated drive.
key_claims: Study 1 (abstract): higher monitoring demands (spatial uncertainty and event rate were manipulated) made hazard detection worse, detection also declined over time on task, and participants reported high workload and stress. Authors conclude safe operation is less likely as monitoring demands rise and drives lengthen, and suggest developers consider countermeasures that reduce drivers' cognitive load. Framing: the vigilance decrement in partially automated vehicles likely reflects driver overload [the 'likely overload' wording comes from the task brief and one search summary; fetched summary only says the study tested whether it reflects overload; uncertain].

Study 2: in a simulated Level 2 drive, response times slowed and hit rates dropped over time in all conditions. A non-driving-related secondary task (occasional general-knowledge yes/no questions) mitigated the decrement; a driving-related secondary task did not (similar to control). Authors conclude both resource depletion and disengagement contribute, and that infrequent, intermittent non-driving breaks may help.
headline_figures: Study 1 (press release only, not the paper's text): accuracy fell 7 to 21 percent over the 40-minute simulation; best early (first 10 min) success about 88 percent. 60 licensed drivers.

Study 2: 117 participants; 45-minute drive; about 1,350 opposite-lane vehicles; 68 hazardous events (about 5 percent signal rate); 4 periods of watch; 8 spoken yes/no questions per secondary-task condition; no significant NASA-TLX workload difference between conditions.
sample_unit_and_population: Study 1: 60 licensed drivers, driving simulator, university-linked. Study 2: 117 participants, mean age 20.5, 86 female, recruited via SONA for course credit, video-based simulation. Neither involves software engineers or AI agents.
observed_vs_stated: Both observed task performance (hit rate, response time, signal detection). Both also collected self-report (workload/stress in study 1; SSSQ and NASA-TLX in study 2). Mechanism claims partly inferred from self-report.
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Study 1: high monitoring demands (spatial uncertainty, event rate) plus time on task producing workload and stress, read by authors as driver overload. Study 2: tested overload vs underload accounts and concluded resource depletion and disengagement both contribute; the task is described as boring but demanding.
consequence_for_quality: Missed hazards that the automation could not detect: lower hit rates and slower responses over time in both studies; study 1 reports every driver missed some hazards (press release).
what_reduces_the_load: Study 1: abstract suggests countermeasures that reduce drivers' cognitive load (no specific design tested, as far as the abstract shows). Study 2: infrequent, intermittent non-driving secondary tasks (breaks) reduced the decrement; driving-related tasks did not.
limitations_stated: Study 2: video-based rather than interactive simulator (no takeover); only one hazard type; very low false alarm rates with high variance so signal-detection measures need caution (summarised from PMC, not verbatim). Study 1: limitations not read (full text unavailable) [uncertain].
counter_evidence: Study 2 itself cuts against a pure overload story: it pitted overload against underload, and adding a small non-driving task helped, while the driving-related task (extra load on the same resource) did not. Authors settle on both resource depletion and disengagement. Study 2 found no workload (NASA-TLX) difference between conditions. A 2024 Human Factors follow-up by the Greenlee group reportedly found the decrement is more severe in automated than manual driving (search result only, not opened).
verification_status: Study 2 claims: checked against PMC full text page (opened). Study 1 abstract claims: checked against Europe PMC abstract record (opened), full paper NOT opened [uncertain for methods/limitations]. Study 1 numbers (7-21 percent, 88 percent, 60 drivers): from Rice press release (opened), not the paper; the 7-21 percent figure is not verified against the paper [uncertain].
usable_claim: Analogy only: automated driving is not agent supervision. In a 2019 Human Factors simulator study, drivers monitoring a partially automated car detected hazards worse when monitoring demands rose and as time on task passed, and reported high workload and stress; the authors suggested cutting cognitive load. A 2023 Human Factors study found a 45-minute monitoring task showed a vigilance decrement that a small, intermittent non-driving task reduced. Reading these as evidence about reviewing AI agent output is the essay's analogy, not the studies' finding.
do_not_use: Do not present the 7-21 percent or 88 percent figures as the paper's own without opening it. Do not say overload is established as the cause (study 2 points to depletion plus disengagement). Do not say these studies concern software, code review or AI agents. Do not generalise from student samples and a video simulation to professionals. Do not say secondary tasks in general help (only the non-driving one did).
